meta.title: FaaSBox — a lightweight Function-as-a-Service platform for TypeScript
meta.description: A lightweight Function-as-a-Service platform for TypeScript, with zero dependencies. Call a function over HTTP or put it on a cron schedule. One Go binary, one SQLite file, nothing else to install.

hero.lead: Write your functions in the browser, then call them over HTTP or put them on a cron schedule. Deploys as a single Docker container: one Go binary, one SQLite file, nothing else to install.

shot.alt: The FaaSBox editor: the function list, the five tabs of a function, its code, and the runner showing a successful run

steps.title: Write, install and test in the browser

bullets.text: The code. Your function reads JSON on stdin and writes JSON on stdout. No framework, no handler signature to memorise, nothing to import.
bullets.alt: The script tab of a function, with its code

bullets.text: package.json — optional. List your npm packages and save; the install runs on the server and you watch it from the tab — installing, then ready, or the tail of the failure if npm had something to say. There is nothing else to set up.
bullets.alt: The package.json tab of a function, listing an npm dependency and showing its install state

bullets.text: Run — one click executes the function and shows you its result, its output and its duration, without leaving the tab.
bullets.alt: The runner toolbar and its Run button

bullets.text: Files — the other tabs show what the database holds; this one shows what the machine has. The folder as it is on disk: your files, the lockfile, and the node_modules the install produced. Read-only, and the place to look when a version is not the one you expected.
bullets.alt: The Files tab of a function, listing its folder on disk

steps.title: Give it a trigger
steps.body: Two ways to start a run, and a function can carry both at once.

ways.text: An HTTP call. POST /invoke/{name} with an API key, created on the API keys page. The request body becomes the function's stdin, and the response carries its result and duration. The editor prints that route under the name of the function you have open, with an example curl next to it: the whole call, ready to copy, the key left as a placeholder.
ways.alt: The API keys page, with the form that creates a key and sets its scope

ways.text: A cron schedule. Added in the Triggers tab: fifteen ready-made expressions, a free field, and a cap on concurrent runs. Changes take effect immediately — nothing restarts.
ways.alt: The Triggers tab of a function, showing a schedule and its payload

steps.title: Read the log
steps.body: Every run records its trigger, status, duration, stdout, stderr, request payload and exit code. Including the runs that never happened: a schedule that came due while the server was down is logged as missed, with the count and the window. A key that may manage functions reads that history over the API too — the only way to see what a cron trigger did without the credentials of the instance itself.

agents.title: An agent can write the functions for you.
agents.lead: FaaSBox speaks MCP at POST /mcp. An agent that connects is handed the writing contract on the spot — payload on stdin, JSON result on stdout, the naming rule, the size caps, the cron format — so “here is a URL and a key, work it out” becomes “write me a function that emails me every morning”.
points: Two ways in. A click: the agent opens a browser on a consent screen that names it and says what it is asking for, you approve, and no secret is pasted anywhere. Or an API key marked Can manage functions, carried in a header — the shape for a non-interactive integration, and the only one on an instance that does not know its own public address.

Both grant the same thing, and that thing is everything. Reading, replacing, running and deleting every function of the instance, and reading their execution history. There is no narrower grant today: a scoped key creates nothing, so an agent that has to create functions holds one that reaches them all. Treat losing either as you would treat losing a shell on the machine.

Seven tools, one per verb. list_functions, get_function, create_function, update_function, delete_function, invoke_function and get_function_logs. Each takes the same code path as its HTTP route, so what an agent may do is exactly what its credential may do — refusals included.

Revocable, from the editor. The AI MCP page lists every agent that authorized itself, the day you approved it and the day its access expires on its own. Revoke takes effect on that agent's next call — there is no session to wait out.

Streamable HTTP, and nothing to install. One endpoint, POST /mcp, on the instance you already deployed. No stdio variant: it would mean shipping an artifact and asking you to run a second runtime next to the first.

storage.title: The database is a single file.
storage.lead: SQLite. Functions, schedules, secrets, keys and logs all live in it, encrypted column by column. No database server to provision, and backing up the instance means copying one file.
storage.boxRemoteFileNote: the same file, kept in sync
storage.noteTitle: Two reasons to turn it on
storage.noteDocker: The disk underneath is not permanent. A container is replaced on every deploy and takes its filesystem with it. Litestream puts the file back before the server starts, so the container stays disposable and your data doesn't.
storage.noteBackup: Or simply as a backup. Even on a server whose disk does survive, the same mirror is an off-site copy that is always current — no dump to schedule, no window during which the last hour is missing. What leaves the machine is ciphertext: keep the key elsewhere and a copy of that bucket opens nothing.
storage.noteOff: Leave it off and nothing else changes: FaaSBox runs from the local file alone, which is what you want on your own machine.
storage.noteDeps: Your dependencies come back on their own, either way. node_modules is not in the file — it is a build artifact, and a heavy one. What is stored is the lockfile, so a fresh container reinstalls exactly the versions the old one ran, before the first call arrives rather than during it.

inside.title: Everything you need, nothing you have to wire up.

cards.title: An editor, not a pipeline
cards.body: Five tabs per function: script, package.json, triggers, secrets, and the files its folder holds on disk. Run executes what the server holds; Save and run appears only when your screen differs from it.

cards.title: Two triggers, one engine
cards.body: An HTTP call and a cron tick take the same path: one Bun subprocess, the same environment, the same ceilings, the same log line. What differs is what happens when the box is busy — HTTP refuses with 429, a cron run waits its turn.

cards.title: Encrypted at rest, not just the secrets
cards.body: AES-256-GCM, column by column: your code, its package.json and lockfile, its triggers, the output of every run, and the secrets you edit as key/value pairs in the Environment tab. One key does all of it, FAASBOX_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and the server will not start without it. The two columns SQL has to look up are encrypted too, and searched through a keyed fingerprint beside them.

cards.title: Keys you can scope
cards.body: Hashed on creation, revealed once, optionally restricted to named functions and given an expiry date. Tick Can manage functions and the key writes them as well as calls them — create, read, replace, delete, and read their history, without the credentials of the instance. An expiry the server can't read is refused at creation rather than quietly dropped.

cards.title: Logs that answer questions
cards.body: Trigger, status, duration, both streams, request payload, exit code, and a flag when something was truncated to fit. Readable from the editor, and over the API with a key that may manage functions. Retention is by row count, purged hourly.

cards.title: Bounded by design
cards.body: Nothing runs unbounded: 30 seconds per run, 1 MB per request body, 1 MB captured per output stream, four concurrent runs. The sizes and the concurrency are defaults you change with an environment variable; the two timeouts are fixed. PocketBase's rate limiter is armed at every boot, so a third wrong password in a row answers 429 — it does not cover /invoke, which the concurrency ceiling bounds instead.

scope.title: Small enough to hold in your head.
scope.lead: Every decision below takes a moving part out. What is left behaves the same way every time, and you can reason about all of it at once.
items: One boundary to secure. A single superuser administers the instance. No permission matrix to audit and no roles: an API key carries two switches — which functions it reaches, and whether it may write them — both set on the page that created it.
Runs are atomic. A call returns a complete result or an error. Nothing to reassemble on the client, no half-written response to detect.
Functions stay independent. Each one is written, invoked and tested on its own. When something breaks there is no hidden call graph to unwind first.
Nothing fires twice behind your back. A schedule missed during downtime is reported, never replayed — the distinction matters when the function bills a customer or sends mail.
One moving part. No control plane, no registry, no broker, no VPC, no serverless.yml. The platform is the container you started, and that is the whole of it.

start.title: One container, one command.
start.thenAdmin: localhost:8080/ — the editor. Sign in with the address and password from the command above; the account is created on first boot.
start.thenEditor: localhost:8080/_/ — the PocketBase admin underneath, if you ever want the raw collections.
start.localBody: Go 1.24+, Bun and Node.js, then bash infra/dev/dev.sh builds the editor and starts the server.
